topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: If a boat capsizes or swamps, what should occupants generally do?
choice_a: Stay with the boat, since most boats retain enough flotation to support people even when capsized or swamped
choice_b: Immediately swim for the nearest shore, no matter the distance
choice_d: Dive underneath the hull to try to right it from below
explanation: Most recreational boats float even when capsized or full of water, and a swamped hull is a much bigger, more visible target for rescuers than a swimmer, so staying with the boat is generally safest.
source_note: General capsizing-response fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: What is the '1-10-1' principle used to teach cold water immersion survival?
choice_a: A rule stating hypothermia cannot occur in water above 1 degree Celsius
choice_b: About 1 minute to control the initial gasp/breathing response, about 10 minutes of meaningful muscle movement before losing dexterity, and about 1 hour before losing consciousness
choice_c: 1 degree of body temperature lost per minute in any water
choice_d: 1 hour to swim 10 miles before hypothermia sets in
explanation: The 1-10-1 principle describes the general timeline of cold water immersion: about 1 minute to get breathing under control, about 10 minutes of useful muscle movement, and roughly 1 hour before losing consciousness, varying by individual and water temperature.
source_note: General cold-water immersion survival fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: What body position is recommended for a single person in cold water wearing a PFD, to help conserve body heat?
choice_a: Floating flat on the back with arms and legs spread wide
choice_b: Removing the PFD to reduce drag
choice_c: The Heat Escape Lessening Posture (HELP): drawing the knees to the chest and arms close to the body
choice_d: Swimming continuously to generate body heat
explanation: HELP position curls the body to protect the head, neck, and torso -- areas of greatest heat loss -- helping conserve core body temperature while waiting for rescue.
source_note: General cold-water immersion fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: What is the 'huddle' position used for when multiple people are in cold water together?
choice_a: Swimming in a single-file line toward shore
choice_b: Spreading out as far apart as possible to be seen more easily
choice_c: Taking turns submerging to warm up
choice_d: Grouping closely together, chest to chest, to conserve collective body heat and stay more visible to rescuers
explanation: The huddle position groups multiple people together to conserve shared body heat and creates a larger, more visible target for search and rescue.
source_note: General cold-water immersion fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: What is the first action a boat operator should take upon discovering a person has fallen overboard?
choice_a: Immediately reduce speed, shift into neutral, and assign someone to keep constant visual contact with the person in the water
choice_b: Continue at current speed while looking for a place to turn around
choice_c: Throw the anchor toward the person as a flotation aid
choice_d: Wait for the person to swim to the boat before taking any action
explanation: Cutting power immediately reduces the risk of propeller injury, and keeping constant eyes on the victim prevents losing track of their position while maneuvering to return.
source_note: General man-overboard response fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: When approaching a person in the water for rescue, from which direction should the boat generally approach?
choice_a: Always approach bow-first at cruising speed
choice_b: From downwind or downcurrent of the victim, approaching slowly with the engine in neutral near the person
choice_d: It does not matter which direction the boat approaches from
explanation: Approaching from downwind/downcurrent lets the wind or current help push the boat toward the victim in a controlled way, and shifting to neutral near the person avoids propeller injury.
source_note: General man-overboard response fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: What is a serious carbon monoxide (CO) risk associated with idling boat engines or generators, particularly near a swim platform?
choice_a: Carbon monoxide is easily detected by its strong odor, so no special precautions are needed
choice_b: Carbon monoxide risk applies only to sailboats
choice_c: 'Teak surfing' or swimming near an idling engine's exhaust can expose a person to lethal concentrations of odorless carbon monoxide
choice_d: Carbon monoxide only accumulates when the boat's engine is completely off
explanation: Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless, and can build up to dangerous levels near a boat's swim platform or exhaust vents, especially when 'teak surfing' or swimming close to a running engine.
source_note: General CO-poisoning fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: What should occupants of an enclosed cabin be aware of regarding carbon monoxide, even at anchor or dockside?
choice_a: CO cannot accumulate in an enclosed cabin under any circumstances
choice_b: CO detectors are unnecessary on boats because CO only forms outdoors
choice_c: CO risk only exists while the vessel is actively underway
choice_d: Exhaust from the boat's own generator or a neighboring boat's engine can seep into an enclosed cabin and accumulate to dangerous levels
explanation: Generator or engine exhaust, including from a nearby vessel, can enter an enclosed cabin and build up to dangerous CO levels even while docked or at anchor, which is why CO detectors are recommended aboard boats with enclosed accommodations.
source_note: General CO-poisoning fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: If a fire breaks out aboard a boat, what should the operator do regarding the boat's heading relative to the wind?
choice_a: Position the boat so the wind blows the fire and smoke away from occupants, when possible
choice_b: Turn directly into the wind so it feeds more air into the fire
choice_c: Stop the boat and shut off all ventilation immediately, regardless of fire location
choice_d: Wind direction has no bearing on fire response aboard a boat
explanation: Maneuvering so the wind carries flames and smoke away from people aboard helps protect occupants while the fire is fought or the vessel is abandoned if necessary.
source_note: General onboard-fire response fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: Before departing on a trip, why is it recommended to leave a float plan with a family member or friend ashore?
choice_a: It is only useful for offshore trips over 50 miles
choice_b: So someone knows the trip's destination, route, and expected return time and can alert authorities if the boat is overdue
choice_c: It is a legal requirement for every trip in California
choice_d: It replaces the need to carry a PFD
explanation: A float plan lets someone ashore notify the Coast Guard or other authorities with specific details if the boat fails to return as expected, greatly speeding a search.
source_note: General float-plan fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: What is 'cold shock response,' and why is it dangerous for a person suddenly immersed in cold water?
choice_a: A warming sensation that occurs after several hours in cold water
choice_b: A reflex that only affects experienced swimmers
choice_c: An involuntary gasp reflex and rapid breathing triggered by sudden cold immersion, which can cause a person to inhale water if their face is submerged
choice_d: A permanent muscle condition unrelated to water temperature
explanation: Sudden cold immersion triggers an involuntary gasp reflex; if the face is underwater at that moment, the person can inhale water and drown within the first minute, which is why a PFD that keeps the face clear of the water is critical.
source_note: General cold-water immersion fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: What is a leading cause of death among boaters who capsize or fall overboard, according to national boating accident data?
choice_c: Carbon monoxide poisoning in every case
choice_d: Drowning, often among people not wearing a PFD
explanation: The large majority of boating fatalities are drownings, and the great majority of those victims were not wearing a PFD at the time of the accident.
source_note: USCG Recreational Boating Statistics, cited in NASBLA-course materials

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: What is a wise precaution for boaters operating in cold water conditions, even if the air temperature feels warm?
choice_a: Wearing a PFD at all times and dressing for water temperature, not air temperature
choice_b: Ignoring water temperature entirely since air temperature is what matters
choice_c: Removing PFDs once the boat is moving to stay cooler
choice_d: Assuming cold water immersion risk only applies in winter months
explanation: Water temperature, not air temperature, determines cold water immersion risk; boaters are taught to 'dress for the water,' not the weather, and to wear PFDs at all times in cold water conditions.
source_note: General cold-water immersion fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: What should boaters do if their vessel runs aground?
choice_a: Ignore it and continue on the original course
choice_b: Check for hull damage and flooding before attempting to power off, since forcing the engine can worsen damage or push the boat further aground
choice_c: Immediately apply full throttle in reverse regardless of the situation
choice_d: Abandon the boat immediately in all cases
explanation: Checking for damage and flooding first helps determine whether it is safe to power off; forcing the engine without assessing the situation can cause further hull damage or push the vessel into a worse position.
source_note: General grounding-response fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: What is the recommended response if a boat begins taking on water faster than it can be bailed or pumped?
choice_a: Increase speed to try to reach shore before sinking, regardless of distance
choice_b: Turn off all electronics to conserve the battery instead of calling for help
choice_c: Call for help immediately (radio, cell phone, or visual distress signals) while attempting to control flooding and preparing to abandon ship if necessary
choice_d: Wait until the boat is nearly sunk before signaling for help
explanation: Early communication of distress -- by radio, phone, or visual signal -- gives rescuers the best chance to respond while the crew also works to control flooding.
source_note: General flooding-emergency fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content

topic: Emergencies: Capsizing, Fire, Overboard & Cold Water
question: Why are PFDs equipped with a whistle or other sound-signaling device useful in an emergency?
choice_a: Whistles are required only for decoration and have no rescue function
choice_b: They replace the need for a PFD to provide flotation
choice_c: They are useful only in daylight conditions
choice_d: They allow a person in the water to signal their location to rescuers, especially when visibility is limited
explanation: A whistle carries farther than the human voice and works in darkness or poor visibility, helping searchers pinpoint a person's location in the water.
source_note: General PFD accessory fundamentals, standard NASBLA-course content
